lessons.title: Making changes

grammar.title: Future continuous and future perfect
grammar.shortAr: المستمر المستقبلي will be doing، والتام المستقبلي will have done
points: Future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an action in progress at a specific future time.
Future perfect (will have + past participle) describes something completed before a future time, often with by.
Other modals can replace will: might be travelling, may have forgotten, should have completed.
In speech, have is usually weak and links to the past participle.
table: This time next year I'll be studying in France.
I'll have saved enough money by June.
She might be swimming at that time.
We should have finished the project by Friday.
exceptions: Use the future perfect, not the future continuous, for results completed before a deadline.
With other modals, keep the same patterns: might be doing / may have done.

vocab.example: A health scare can transform your lifestyle.
I do a regular workout twice a week.

lessons.title: Sleep
goals: Learn vocabulary about sleep and sleep problems
Use it + passive to report general beliefs
Write an article with linkers that add ideas

grammar.title: Passives for general beliefs
grammar.shortAr: المبني للمجهول مع it: it is believed/thought/suggested that ...
points: Use the passive to focus on the action or the person affected rather than the doer.
For current beliefs: It is thought/believed/expected/reported + that-clause.
For past beliefs use It was thought/expected; for recent claims use It has been suggested/reported.
That can be omitted in less formal English.
table: It is believed that most adults need eight hours' sleep.
It is thought that naps improve alertness.
It has been suggested that screens affect sleep.
It was expected that the clock change would affect health.
The theory has been disproven by researchers.
exceptions: Use a singular passive verb after it.
This structure is more common in formal writing than in conversation.

vocab.example: I drop off as soon as my head hits the pillow.
I'm a light sleeper, so any noise wakes me.
He's a heavy sleeper and sleeps through alarms.
An insomniac often has trouble falling asleep.
I have a short nap in the afternoon.
My neighbour snores loudly.
I woke up after a nightmare.
I overslept and missed my train.
The noise kept me awake.

lessons.title: Keep moving
goals: Express agreement, partial agreement and disagreement

grammar.title: Agreeing and disagreeing
grammar.shortAr: الاتفاق والاختلاف: I couldn't agree more / up to a point / on the other hand
points: Use direct phrases to agree strongly or disagree completely.
For partial agreement use I agree up to a point, but ... or I suppose so, but ... .
Acknowledge an opposing view with That's a fair point, although ... or on the other hand.
Introduce your own opinion with In my opinion, From my perspective or As far as I'm concerned.
table: I agree with you up to a point, but ...
That's a fair point, although it could be argued that ...
In my opinion, everyone should move more.
exceptions: I couldn't agree more means complete agreement, not disagreement.
In phrases of partial agreement, the word point is usually stressed.

vocab.example: Adults should do 150 minutes of moderate exercise weekly.
Vigorous exercise raises the heart rate quickly.
Cycling improves stamina.
Weight training builds strength.
Yoga improves flexibility.
Swimming is a low-impact activity.
Running is a high-impact exercise.
Jogging is an aerobic exercise.
Finding an enjoyable activity is the key to motivation.

reading.summary: An article recommends a weekly mix of moderate or vigorous exercise, strength work, aerobic activity and flexibility training, and notes that fewer than half of adults worldwide do enough.

practice.why: Aerobic exercise such as jogging builds stamina.

lessons.title: Ancient traditions

grammar.title: Phrases related to time
grammar.shortAr: تعبيرات زمنية: just in time for، time is running out، under threat، window of opportunity
points: Use time phrases to say when something must happen or that time is limited.
Just in time for means arriving at the right moment before an event.
Time is running out means little time remains; not a moment too soon means just soon enough.
A window of opportunity is a short period when action is possible; under threat means in danger.
table: They arrived just in time for the bloom.
Time is running out for the beekeepers.
We have a small window of opportunity to act.
The rain came, not a moment too soon.
It's time to move on to the next field.
exceptions: Not a moment too soon means just in time, not 'too late'.
Use time is running out for a person or situation.

vocab.example: We got there just in time for the show.
Time is running out to save the bees.
The tradition is under threat from tourism.
We have a short window of opportunity.
